chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Factors? Foundations of Factor Investing

lessons.title: The Anatomy of a Factor: What Makes a Characteristic 'Priced'

body.text: A factor's history of outperformance is not proof it will keep working. It is a bet, on a risk, a bias, or a friction, that has not gone away yet. Knowing which kind of bet you are making is what separates a systematic strategy from a coincidence that happened to survive one backtest.

children.text: The last lesson established that factors are real, measurable, and already tradeable through NSE factor indices. But it skipped a harder question: why should the market let a factor earn a persistent premium at all? If a large number of NSE and BSE participants know that small, cheap, high-momentum stocks have historically outperformed, shouldn't they simply buy those stocks until the extra return disappears? That it has not disappeared, not fully, for sixty years across value, and thirty years across momentum, is exactly what economists have spent decades arguing about. This lesson walks through the three competing camps of explanation, and then opens up the actual mechanics of how a factor premium gets built into a tradeable portfolio.
Three Competing Explanations for Why Factor Premiums Exist

Financial economists broadly split factor premiums into three types of explanation. They are not mutually exclusive, and for most factors, all three play some role, but which camp you believe shapes how much you trust a factor to survive into the future.
Camp 1: Risk-Based Explanations

markDefs.definition: The heightened risk of financial trouble, earnings collapse, or bankruptcy that value stocks, being cheap for a fundamental reason, tend to carry relative to growth stocks.

children.text: Eugene Fama and Kenneth French argued the value and size premiums are compensation for bearing extra risk. Cheap, small, unloved companies are cheap partly because they are genuinely riskier: thinner balance sheets, less diversified revenue, and a higher chance of underperforming badly in a downturn. This is sometimes called
distress risk

. Under this camp, the value and size premiums are not free money, they are the market's fair price for holding a riskier basket of stocks, and there is no reason to expect the premium to vanish, because the underlying risk has not vanished.

India offers a sharp illustration. Through 2017, small and midcap NSE stocks rallied hard and the size premium looked like easy money. Then in 2018, a wave of credit stress triggered by the IL&FS default hit small and midcap names disproportionately, and many midcap and smallcap indices fell 30 to 40 percent from their peaks while the Nifty 50 held up far better. Investors who had been collecting the small-cap premium for two years got a brutal reminder of exactly what risk they had been paid to carry.
Camp 2: Behavioral Explanations

markDefs.definition: The tendency of investors to project a company's recent growth or decline far into the future, causing them to overpay for 'story' stocks with strong recent narratives and underpay for boring, out-of-favour ones.

children.text: A competing camp, led by Josef Lakonishok, Andrei Shleifer, and Robert Vishny in a 1994 paper, argued the value premium is not compensation for risk at all. It is the reward for exploiting other investors'
extrapolation bias

, the habit of assuming a hot growth stock will keep growing and a struggling company will keep struggling, long after the fundamentals stop supporting that story. Value stocks are cheap not because they are riskier, in this view, but because they have been unfairly punished by investors chasing a narrative, and the value premium is simply the correction that follows when reality reasserts itself.

Momentum has its own behavioral story, and its own discovery date. Narasimhan Jegadeesh and Sheridan Titman first documented the momentum effect in 1993, four years before Mark Carhart built it into a tradeable four-factor model. Their explanation was underreaction: markets are slow to fully price in good or bad news, so a stock that has recently outperformed tends to keep drifting upward for months as the rest of the market catches up. India's retail options and momentum trading boom, and SEBI's repeated public warnings about retail losses chasing story stocks and momentum rallies in the small and microcap segment, are a live version of the same underreaction and herding dynamic academics were describing in US data decades earlier.
Camp 3: Structural and Institutional Frictions

markDefs.definition: The tendency of many real-world investors, especially institutions barred from using leverage by their mandate, to buy risky, high-beta stocks directly instead of borrowing to lever up safer, low-beta stocks, which bids up high-beta names and depresses their forward returns.

children.text: The third camp blames neither pure risk nor investor psychology, but the rules institutions operate under. Andrea Frazzini and Lasse Pedersen's 2014 paper 'Betting Against Beta' argued that many large investors, mutual funds, pension funds, insurance companies, are constrained from using leverage. If such an investor wants a higher return, the mandate-compliant way to get it is not to borrow and buy safe, low-beta stocks, it is to buy risky, high-beta stocks outright. This concentrated demand for high-beta names bids their price up and their future return down, which is exactly why low-volatility stocks have historically delivered better risk-adjusted returns than CAPM would predict. Frazzini and Pedersen called this
leverage aversion

India's own regulatory structure adds a second, homegrown friction. SEBI's 2017 mutual fund categorisation circular defines large-cap as the top 100 companies by market capitalisation, mid-cap as ranks 101 to 250, and small-cap as everything below that, and requires large-cap and mid-cap schemes to hold a minimum proportion of their respective category. This creates mechanical, rules-driven demand for stocks purely because of where they sit in a market-cap ranking, independent of valuation or quality, a structural flow that has nothing to do with risk or behavioral bias and everything to do with how Indian mutual fund mandates are written.

body.title: Show me the math: how Betting Against Beta is actually constructed

children.text: A BAB portfolio cannot simply be long low-beta stocks and short high-beta stocks in equal rupee amounts, because that leaves you with an overall low-beta, defensive portfolio rather than a factor that isolates the leverage-aversion effect. Instead, each leg is rescaled to have a beta of exactly 1 before combining them.

content.caption: R_L and R_H are the returns of the low-beta and high-beta legs; beta_L and beta_H are their respective betas

children.text: Dividing the low-beta leg's excess return by its own beta is mathematically equivalent to leveraging it up to a beta of 1. Dividing the high-beta leg by its beta de-leverages it down to a beta of 1. The result is a beta-neutral, self-financing portfolio: on paper, you are borrowing to lever the safe stocks and using the proceeds of shorting the leveraged-down risky stocks to fund it. If leverage-averse institutions really are overpaying for high-beta names, this portfolio should earn a positive average return, and in the original 2014 study, across multiple markets and asset classes, it did.

body.caption: The three camps, side by side

cells: The premium is fair compensation for a genuinely riskier basket of stocks
The premium exists because other investors are systematically biased, not because the stocks are riskier
Lakonishok, Shleifer, Vishny (1994); Jegadeesh and Titman (1993)
The premium exists because of mandate constraints or rules that create mechanical demand or supply imbalances

body.text: Notice that value shows up under both the risk-based and behavioral camps. This is not a contradiction, it is the actual state of the academic debate: the same historical premium can plausibly be explained by two very different mechanisms, and thirty years later, economists still have not fully settled which one dominates. When you cannot tell whether a premium is risk or bias, you should size your position as if it could be either, and never assume it is a free lunch.

children.text: The Anatomy of a Factor Portfolio: How the Premium Gets Built in Practice

Understanding why a factor might earn a premium is only half the job. The other half is mechanical: turning a characteristic like 'cheapness' or 'momentum' into an actual portfolio you could run on NSE-listed stocks. Every factor portfolio, whatever the underlying characteristic, is built from the same five decisions.

body.caption: The five construction choices behind every factor portfolio

cells: Which stocks are even eligible, often filtered for a minimum market capitalisation and trading liquidity on the NSE, so the strategy is not built on illiquid, hard-to-trade names
The raw signal used to rank every eligible stock, such as price-to-book for value or six-month price return for momentum
Where the ranked list gets cut, common choices are top and bottom thirds (terciles), fifths (quintiles), or tenths (deciles)
A long-only fund simply overweights the top bucket; an academic or hedge-fund style factor portfolio goes long the top bucket and short the bottom bucket
Equal-weighting every stock in the bucket versus market-cap weighting it, and how often the portfolio is reconstructed, monthly, quarterly, or annually

children.text: Two identical characteristics, ranked identically, can produce meaningfully different portfolios depending purely on these mechanical choices. A quintile-based value strategy rebalanced quarterly and an equal-weighted decile-based value strategy rebalanced annually are both 'value factor' strategies, but they will not hold the same stocks, will not have the same turnover, and will not deliver the same real-world return after costs. Chapter 3 of this course walks through exactly how to make each of these choices for the factors you will build yourself.

body.title: Which Camp Do You Trust?
body.scenario: It is early 2018. Small and midcap NSE stocks have just delivered three straight years of outperformance over the Nifty 50, and several new smallcap-focused funds have launched to capture the trend. A junior analyst on your desk argues this outperformance is 'basically guaranteed to continue' because small caps have beaten large caps historically over multi-decade periods.
body.prompt: Using the three-camp framework from this lesson, what is the flaw in the analyst's reasoning, and what actually happened to small and midcap NSE stocks later that year?
body.modelAnswer: The analyst is treating the small-cap premium as if it were a free, guaranteed payout, when the risk-based camp's explanation is precisely that small caps earn more because they carry more risk, not despite it. Three good years does not remove that risk, it just means the risk has not shown up yet. Later in 2018, the IL&FS default triggered a credit crisis that hit small and midcap names especially hard, and many small and midcap indices fell 30 to 40 percent from their highs while the Nifty 50 held up far better, which is exactly the kind of drawdown the risk-based explanation predicts investors should eventually be paid to absorb. A well-calibrated analyst would frame the historical premium as compensation for a real risk that can materialise sharply and without much warning, not as a guaranteed trend.

body.title: Test Yourself: Matching Camps to Mechanisms
body.question: The low-volatility anomaly, where low-beta stocks deliver better risk-adjusted returns than CAPM predicts, is best explained by which camp?
options: Risk-based: low-beta stocks are secretly riskier than they appear
Behavioral: investors systematically underreact to news about low-beta companies
Structural: leverage-averse institutions bid up high-beta stocks instead of borrowing to lever safe ones, depressing high-beta forward returns
None of the three camps have a credible explanation for this anomaly
body.explanation: Frazzini and Pedersen's 'Betting Against Beta' (2014) is the structural/frictions explanation: because many institutions cannot use leverage, they buy high-beta stocks directly to seek higher returns instead of levering up low-beta stocks, which bids up high-beta prices and depresses their forward returns relative to what CAPM would predict.

body.title: Vocabulary Check: Terms From This Lesson

cards.definition: The heightened risk of financial trouble or bankruptcy that value stocks tend to carry, used by Fama and French to argue the value premium is compensation for genuine risk.
The tendency of investors to project recent growth or decline far into the future, causing systematic overpricing of 'story' stocks and underpricing of out-of-favour ones.
The tendency of leverage-constrained institutions to buy high-beta stocks directly instead of borrowing to lever up low-beta stocks, depressing high-beta forward returns.
A beta-neutral factor portfolio, long a leveraged low-beta leg and short a de-leveraged high-beta leg, designed by Frazzini and Pedersen (2014) to isolate the leverage-aversion effect.
The cutoff points, such as terciles, quintiles, or deciles, used to divide a ranked list of stocks into the buckets that form a factor portfolio.

body.text: Historical episodes referenced in this lesson, including the 2018 small and midcap drawdown following the IL&FS default, are described for educational illustration only and are not a forecast or recommendation regarding any current or future market segment. Always verify SEBI circulars and index methodology details directly with SEBI and NSE Indices Limited before relying on them.

points: Factor premiums are explained by three competing, overlapping camps: risk-based, behavioral, and structural/institutional

Risk-based explanations (Fama and French) treat premiums like value and size as fair compensation for genuinely riskier stocks, illustrated by the 2018 small and midcap drawdown after the IL&FS default
Behavioral explanations (Lakonishok, Shleifer, Vishny 1994 on value; Jegadeesh and Titman 1993 on momentum) attribute premiums to investor extrapolation bias and underreaction rather than risk
Structural explanations (Frazzini and Pedersen's Betting Against Beta, 2014) attribute the low-volatility anomaly to leverage-averse institutions bidding up high-beta stocks
India has its own structural frictions, including SEBI's 2017 mutual fund categorisation rules that create mechanical, mandate-driven demand tied to market-cap rank

Every factor portfolio, regardless of the underlying characteristic, is built from five mechanical choices: universe, characteristic and ranking, breakpoints, long-only vs long-short, and weighting and rebalancing frequency
